metadata.title: MU Vs Its Peers: A Lead With A Price Tag

content.text:
After a stunning +749% run over the last twelve months, Micron Technology (MU) stock has recently pulled back, trading at about $959.48 a share. The company sits at the heart of the AI buildout, supplying the critical memory chips that power modern data centers. Yet for investors, its position within its competitive group presents a puzzle. Micron trades at a premium 44.8 times earnings, more expensive than rival NVIDIA's 32.3 multiple, but its operating margin of 48% doesn't reach NVIDIA's 64%.
This raises a sharp question for anyone sizing up the semiconductor space: Is paying a premium price for a company that isn't the premium performer the right call?
Micron Is Priced Near The Top, But Does Not Lead The Pack.
Among its direct competitors, Micron holds a strong but not dominant position. Its price-to-earnings multiple is the second highest in its peer group, trailing only Advanced Micro Devices, which trades at 179.8 times earnings. Micron is valued more richly than NVIDIA, Western Digital at 29.4 times earnings, and Qualcomm at a modest 18.9 times.
On the delivery side, the story is similar. While its revenue grew an impressive 86% over the last twelve months, its operating margin of 48% is second best. Here again, NVIDIA leads the group with a commanding 64% operating margin. Micron is a powerful player, but on the two core measures of price and profitability, at least one peer has it beat.
New Contracts Promise Stability, But May Cap The Upside.
The market's willingness to award Micron a premium valuation hinges on a fundamental shift in its business model. Management recently announced it has signed 16 strategic customer agreements, or SCAs. These are not loose arrangements; they are structured as "take or pay agreements with binding commitments to purchase specific volumes over this multiyear term." For a historically cyclical industry, this introduces an unprecedented level of predictability.
These agreements create a powerful floor under the business. Management states the floor price in these deals "enables a very robust gross margin for Micron, well above our peak quarterly margins in any past cycle." This change is central to the debate over whether Micron has finally shed its boom-and-bust reputation. A recent analysis asks a similar question, exploring if Micron's old cycle is truly broken.
